column2: Shaffer & Ginsberg 2017, Frontiers in Public Health
column3: RMSSD is the primary time-domain measure of short-term heart rate variability. It reflects vagally mediated, beat-to-beat changes in heart rhythm, and is the HRV metric least affected by breathing rate.

Short-term HRV is conventionally measured over five minutes. Shorter recordings can give reliable RMSSD from about sixty seconds, but SDNN over one minute is not comparable to published five-minute norms.

column2: Shaffer & Ginsberg 2017, Frontiers in Public Health
column3: Vagal tone indexed by HRV is associated with the capacity to regulate physiological arousal and to recover after it. It varies substantially between individuals, which is why an absolute value says much less than a change against a person's own usual.

Ectopic beats and missed detections inflate RMSSD dramatically, because the metric is built from successive differences. Editing is required before the number means anything, and heavy editing biases the result low.

In a large accelerometry cohort, sleep regularity predicted all-cause mortality more strongly than sleep duration did. Regularity here means the consistency of sleep and wake timing, not the number of hours.

Irregular sleep timing has been associated with risk across a wide range of conditions, in some analyses more than short sleep duration. Timing and duration are separate things and can move independently.

Digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia reduces sleep-onset latency and wake-after-sleep-onset against inactive controls. Against active controls the difference is not significant, which is a caution about attributing effects to any single component.

column2: Shaffer & Ginsberg 2017, Frontiers in Public Health
column3: Resting heart rate and HRV are related but not interchangeable. Resting heart rate is a single rate; HRV describes the variation around it, and the two can move in different directions.

Behavioural activation is among the simplest well-evidenced treatments for low mood. Its mechanism is that action precedes mood rather than waiting on it, which is why the size of the action matters less than its occurrence.

In a three-arm randomised trial of adaptive messaging, the reinforcement-learning arm increased daily steps substantially more than fixed or random schedules. The measured outcome was steps, not mood.

Momentary affect is commonly described on two axes rather than one: how pleasant an experience feels, and how activated it is. Flat-and-low and tense-and-low are distinct states that a single mood scale cannot separate.

column2: Circumplex model of affect, arousal dimension
column3: Arousal describes how activated or energised an experience is, independently of whether it feels pleasant. High arousal covers both agitation and enthusiasm; low arousal covers both calm and lethargy, which is why it is measured separately from valence.

Momentary assessment samples experience in the moment rather than by recall, which avoids the reconstruction errors of retrospective report. Signals scattered within blocks are used so a person cannot anticipate the prompt and pre-compose an answer.

column2: Müller, Harari et al. 2021, Scientific Reports
column3: A GPS-mobility model for depression scored an area under the curve of 0.82 in a homogeneous sample of 57 students and 0.57, which is chance, in a heterogeneous sample of 5262. Models fitted across people do not transfer to individuals.

column2: Henson, Torous et al. 2023, npj Schizophrenia
column3: Anomaly detection against a person's own passive-data baseline was more frequent in the month before relapse than at other times. Within-person deviation generalises better than cross-person prediction.

column2: JMIR 2025 review, mobile sensing for depression
column3: Across nine studies of mobile sensing for depression, most could predict symptom severity to some degree, but only one could distinguish worsening from relapse from recovery. The clinically actionable distinction remains largely unsolved.

A six-second delay before opening a chosen application led participants to abandon 36% of open attempts, and total open attempts fell over six weeks. The mechanism is habit decay rather than willpower.

column2: Meinhardt, Purohit, Rukzio et al. 2025, CHI
column3: Intervention effectiveness during scrolling is context-dependent. Sleepiness lowers reactance, low mood at home slows responsiveness, and people desensitise to prompts that ignore context.
Effects of repeated prompting decay over time in multiple micro-randomised trials, and some show null results at follow-up. Habituation is the most consistent finding in this literature.

A meta-analysis of 176 randomised trials found small effects for mental-health apps: g of about 0.28 for depression and 0.26 for anxiety. Effects were larger where apps included CBT components or mood monitoring.
Across 93 mental-health apps, median fifteen-day retention was under four percent and median use was about five sessions. Anything depending on a person opening an app inherits this.

column2: Fitz, Kushlev, Ariely et al. 2019, Computers in Human Behavior
column3: In a randomised trial, receiving notifications in three daily batches left participants happier, less stressed and more attentive than receiving them as they arrived. The mediator was subjective attention quality.
Removing colour from a phone display reduces screen time in controlled trials. The proposed mechanism is that colour carries much of what makes a feed engaging, rather than any change in intention.
Unfinished tasks intrude on cognition until they are resolved. Writing a specific plan for the unfinished task reduces the intrusion about as effectively as completing it does.

A phone camera with the torch lit can record the pulse waveform at a fingertip, from which beat-to-beat intervals and short-term HRV can be derived. Signal quality, not sensor precision, is the limiting factor.

Beat-template correlation is used to decide whether a photoplethysmography recording is trustworthy. Physiological plausibility of intervals alone is insufficient, because noise can produce plausible-looking rates.

column2: Thayer & Lane 2000, Journal of Affective Disorders
column3: The neurovisceral integration model links heart rate variability to the brain systems involved in flexibly regulating attention and emotion. In this account, vagally mediated HRV indexes how readily the nervous system can adapt to changing demands.

Heart rate variability biofeedback trains slow breathing at roughly six breaths per minute, the rate at which heart rhythm oscillations resonate. Regular practice raises baroreflex gain, and the breathing rate matters more than any device used to find it.

column2: Zaccaro et al. 2018, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
column3: A systematic review of slow-breathing studies found that breathing below ten breaths per minute increases heart rate variability and EEG alpha power, alongside reports of greater comfort and relaxation and reduced arousal.

Restricting sleep to six hours a night for two weeks produced cognitive deficits equivalent to two nights of total sleep deprivation. Participants' own ratings of sleepiness levelled off after a few days, while their measured performance kept declining — the impairment outpaced the awareness of it.

Reading on a light-emitting device before bed, compared with a printed book, suppressed melatonin, delayed the circadian clock, lengthened the time taken to fall asleep, and reduced next-morning alertness in a controlled crossover study.

column2: Drake et al. 2013, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine
column3: Caffeine taken as long as six hours before bedtime measurably disrupted sleep in a placebo-controlled trial, reducing recorded sleep by about an hour, while participants' own estimates of the disruption were smaller than the objective loss.

column2: Ebrahim et al. 2013, Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research
column3: A review of polysomnography studies found alcohol before bed shortens the time to fall asleep but disrupts the second half of the night, reducing REM sleep — sleep arrives faster and finishes worse.

Social jetlag names the discrepancy between the sleep timing a person's body clock runs and the timing their weekday obligations impose, measured as the shift between workday and free-day sleep. It behaves like a small weekly time-zone crossing taken without travelling.

column2: Baron et al. 2017, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine
column3: Case reports describe people whose pursuit of perfect sleep-tracker numbers worsened their sleep, a pattern the authors named orthosomnia. Tracker sleep staging is imperfect, and treating its nightly score as a target rather than a rough record inverted the tool's purpose.

A dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts found the largest mental-health differences between no activity and modest amounts, with diminishing returns beyond. Accumulating activity equivalent to brisk walking for about two and a half hours a week marked most of the observed difference.

column2: Schuch et al. 2018, American Journal of Psychiatry
column3: Across prospective cohort studies with over two hundred sixty thousand participants, people with higher baseline physical activity had meaningfully lower odds of developing low mood over the following years, an association that held across ages and continents.

A ninety-minute walk in a natural setting, compared with an equally long walk beside traffic, reduced self-reported rumination and activity in a prefrontal region associated with it. The walks were matched for physical effort; the surroundings were the manipulated variable.

In a sample of nearly twenty thousand people, those reporting at least a hundred and twenty minutes of nature contact per week reported better health and wellbeing than those with none. The pattern held whether the time came in one visit or many.

column2: Burns et al. 2021, Journal of Affective Disorders
column3: In UK Biobank data, each additional hour of self-reported daytime outdoor light was associated with better mood, easier waking, and lower odds of long-term low mood, consistent with daylight's role in setting the circadian clock.

A meta-analysis of a hundred and forty-eight studies found that stronger social relationships predicted substantially better survival over time — an influence on mortality comparable in size to established behavioural risk factors such as smoking cessation's benefit.

column2: Emmons & McCullough 2003, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
column3: Participants randomly assigned to list things they were grateful for each week reported better mood and fewer physical complaints over the following weeks than those assigned to list burdens or neutral events.

A meta-analysis of a hundred and forty-six experiments on expressive writing — writing privately about difficult experiences for a few sessions — found small but reliable benefits across psychological and physical health measures.

column2: Goyal et al. 2014, JAMA Internal Medicine
column3: A systematic review of forty-seven randomised trials found mindfulness meditation programmes produced small-to-moderate improvements in anxiety, low mood and pain over about eight weeks, with little evidence that they outperformed active treatments such as exercise.

column2: Topp et al. 2015, Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics
column3: The WHO-5 is a five-item wellbeing index scored zero to a hundred, validated across a wide range of study fields. It asks about the last two weeks, and its brevity and positive phrasing were deliberate design choices to make repeated use tolerable.

column2: Shiffman, Stone & Hufford 2008, Annual Review of Clinical Psychology
column3: Ecological momentary assessment gathers reports of experience in the moment, in a person's own settings, precisely because retrospective summaries are systematically distorted by memory — by peaks, by endings, and by the mood present at recall.

column2: Stothart, Mitchum & Yehnert 2015, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
column3: Merely receiving a notification, without ever attending to it, impaired performance on an attention task about as much as actively using the phone — the thought of the unchecked alert did the damage.

column2: Ward et al. 2017, Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
column3: The mere presence of a person's own silent phone on the desk, versus in another room, measurably reduced available working memory capacity in experiments — even when participants reported not thinking about it.

column2: Hunt et al. 2018, Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
column3: Undergraduates randomly assigned to limit social media to thirty minutes a day for three weeks reported lower loneliness and lower low mood than a use-as-usual group, with the largest changes among those who began most affected.

column2: Allcott et al. 2020, American Economic Review
column3: Paying people to deactivate a social network for four weeks in a large randomised trial increased offline activity and small but measurable subjective wellbeing, and the deactivated group used the network less after the study ended.

column2: Nolen-Hoeksema et al. 2008, Perspectives on Psychological Science
column3: Rumination is repetitive, passive thinking about distress, its causes and its consequences, without moving to action. Studies following people over time find it prolongs low periods and predicts their recurrence, distinguishing it from reflection that resolves.

In the COBRA randomised trial of four hundred forty adults, behavioural activation delivered by junior mental-health workers was not inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered by psychological therapists — a structurally simpler treatment matched a more complex one.
